How elected leaders can dismantle democracy A government can hold elections while making it harder for the opposition to win. Courts can remain open while protecting those in power. Newspapers can still appear while their owners face pressure to stay silent. Democratic institutions can survive in name while losing their purpose.
This is the central warning of How Democracies Die. Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt argue that elected leaders can gradually destroy the system that brought them to office. Political parties must resist such leaders, and constitutional rules need support from shared standards of conduct.
Published in 2018, the book draws on European and Latin American history to examine the United States during Donald Trump’s rise and first year as president. This summary presents that argument in its original setting. It does not treat later events as evidence the authors already possessed. Harvard’s publication record confirms the book’s authors, date, and comparative scope.
Why decline can be hard to recognize The authors contrast an obvious military takeover with a gradual loss of democratic competition. In the second pattern, each measure can look temporary, technical, or lawful. Officials may describe attacks on independent institutions as efforts to improve efficiency or fight corruption.
Venezuela illustrates the danger. Hugo Chávez won the presidency in 1998 by challenging a discredited political establishment. Over time, his government delayed a recall referendum, blacklisted people who signed the recall petition, expanded control over the supreme court, and restricted independent media. Elections continued, but the conditions for competition became increasingly unequal. The publisher’s excerpt traces this progression.
The distinction matters because democracy requires more than counting votes. Citizens need meaningful choices, basic freedoms, and a fair chance to replace their leaders. A single election victory gives a government authority to govern. It does not give it permission to remove those conditions.
Four warning signs of authoritarian behavior Drawing on political scientist Juan Linz, the authors identify four warning signs. Their test concerns observable conduct rather than a candidate’s ideology or personal charm.
Warning sign What readers should examine Weak commitment to democratic rules Does the leader reject constitutional limits or refuse to accept credible election results? Rejection of opponents’ legitimacy Does the leader portray lawful rivals as enemies who have no right to govern? Acceptance of political violence Does the leader encourage attacks or excuse violence by supporters? Willingness to restrict civil liberties Does the leader threaten the freedoms of critics, opponents, or the press? The authors say any one of these signs warrants concern. In their assessment, Trump’s 2016 campaign displayed all four. That is their explicit judgment, rather than a neutral classification accepted by everyone. Their published interview explains the test and its application.
The test is a warning system, not proof that dictatorship must follow. A useful application is to ask the same questions about one’s preferred candidate. Otherwise, the checklist can become another way to condemn political opponents while overlooking similar conduct among allies.
Political parties control an important entrance Dangerous leaders rarely gain power entirely on their own. Established politicians can lend them access, organization, and respectability. They may expect to control the newcomer or use the newcomer’s popularity against a shared opponent.
The book examines this mistake through the rise of Hitler and Mussolini. The authors focus on decisions by established leaders who helped them reach office. The lesson concerns the failure of political judgment; it does not require treating every later demagogue as identical to either dictator.
Parties serve as gatekeepers when they refuse nominations, endorsements, and alliances to figures who reject democratic competition. The difficult test comes when exclusion carries a political cost. Protecting democracy may require supporting a rival who accepts its rules. The publisher’s teaching guide highlights these choices.
This creates a real tension. Party leaders can also protect insiders and exclude legitimate challengers. A democratic party therefore needs a defensible boundary: challenging a policy or establishment is different from rejecting opponents’ right to compete.
How incumbents make competition unfair Once in office, an aspiring autocrat can weaken checks on power through three connected methods. Ziblatt describes them in his interview with California magazine.
Control the referees. Courts, prosecutors, election authorities, and other public bodies should apply rules independently. Loyal appointments and selective enforcement can turn them into tools against rivals and protection for the government.
Weaken the opposition. Independent journalists, civic groups, business leaders, and opposition politicians can face pressure. The aim may be silence or dependence rather than an outright ban.
Change the rules. Electoral laws and other arrangements can be altered to favor the incumbent. Competition remains possible, but the governing party makes its own defeat less likely.
These methods reinforce one another. A weakened court offers less protection to a targeted newspaper. A quieter press makes changes to electoral rules harder to scrutinize.
Consider a hypothetical local election. A mayor replaces independent election officials with loyalists, threatens a critical newspaper’s access to public advertising, and changes registration procedures to burden opposition neighborhoods. Each act requires separate investigation. Together, they raise a larger question about fair competition. This is an illustration of the framework, not a case reported in the book.
Two unwritten rules help institutions work Levitsky and Ziblatt emphasize two norms that support constitutional government. They call these democracy’s informal guardrails.
Mutual toleration means accepting lawful opponents as legitimate participants. Parties can disagree strongly while recognizing each other’s right to compete and govern.
Institutional forbearance means using legal powers with restraint. Officials avoid exploiting every available procedure to disable their rivals or make ordinary government impossible.
The norms support each other. If losing means handing power to a legitimate rival, restraint is easier. If losing feels like national destruction, extreme tactics become easier to justify. Opponents then respond, and the conflict escalates. The authorized excerpt in Pomona College Magazine explains this relationship.
Forbearance still leaves room for serious oversight. Investigating misconduct or imposing a justified sanction can protect democracy. The practical judgment concerns purpose, evidence, and consequences. Restraint cannot mean giving officials immunity from accountability.
America’s stability had an exclusionary foundation The authors complicate any nostalgic appeal to a more civil political past. After Reconstruction, Southern states stripped Black citizens of voting rights. National political cooperation coexisted with entrenched racial exclusion. The publisher’s teaching guide identifies this as a central theme of the book.
Civil rights gains later changed the political system. As voters increasingly sorted into parties by race, religion, and culture, policy disagreements became tied to identity and status. In the authors’ account, fears of losing social dominance helped drive Republican radicalization. They place substantial responsibility on Republican leaders while also describing cycles of retaliation. Their 2018 Harvard interview develops this explanation.
Their goal is inclusive democracy with durable restraint. Restoring calm by sacrificing equal participation would defeat that goal. This is one of the book’s strongest qualifications: political stability and democratic equality are distinct achievements, and both need protection.
Defending democracy requires alliances and choices The authors recommend broad coalitions that cross ordinary political divisions. Business, religious, civic, and party leaders can disagree on policy while defending fair elections and independent institutions. They also connect lasting democratic repair with reducing economic inequality and building a more inclusive politics.
Their Harvard interview urges active opposition through elections, courts, and legislatures while those channels remain available. It also acknowledges that responding to repeated norm violations involves difficult choices. Automatic retaliation can deepen the damage, while continued restraint can leave abuses unchecked.
A practical reading of this argument is to judge reforms by what they permit future opponents to do. Would a proposed power still seem acceptable if a rival used it? Would an election rule still seem fair after one’s own party lost? These questions do not settle every dispute. They help distinguish durable democratic safeguards from temporary partisan advantages.
What the framework can and cannot explain The book’s strength is its attention to decisions that occur before a visible collapse. It directs readers toward party alliances, official appointments, enforcement, and political language. These choices are easier to examine than a vague claim that a country has become authoritarian.
Its comparisons require care. Different countries have different courts, party systems, histories, and sources of power. Similar rhetoric does not prove an identical outcome. Nor does the checklist establish a numerical probability of democratic failure.
My main reservation concerns the boundary between restraint and necessary reform. An old practice can protect fair competition, preserve exclusion, or do both. Readers must ask who benefits from a norm and whose rights it protects. The authors’ own discussion of racial exclusion makes that question unavoidable.
The framework is most useful for examining specific conduct. A present-day assessment needs additional evidence about actual enforcement, electoral fairness, civil liberties, and the ability to remove those in office. The book supplies questions for that work; its 2018 diagnosis cannot substitute for it.
Sources Harvard Weatherhead Center: publication record and scope. Penguin Random House: authorized excerpt and teaching guide. History News Network: interview with both authors. California: interview with Daniel Ziblatt, January 2018. Pomona College Magazine: authorized book excerpt. Harvard Gazette: interview with both authors, January 2018.

How Governments Became Powerful, Lawful, and Accountable A government needs enough power to enforce decisions. People also need protection from that power. Francis Fukuyama’s The Origins of Political Order: From Prehuman Times to the French Revolution explains how societies developed institutions to meet these competing needs.
His central argument is that effective liberal government combines three distinct achievements: a capable state, the rule of law, and political accountability. These institutions have different origins. They can develop separately, support one another, or come into conflict.
This is the first volume of a larger study. It follows political development from early human societies to the eve of the French Revolution. China, India, the Muslim world, and Europe supply its main comparisons. The author’s overview makes this scope clear. The book explains how institutions emerged, rather than offering a universal sequence that every country must follow.
Three Institutions, Three Different Jobs Fukuyama separates questions that political debate often combines:
Institution Main task What can go wrong without it? A capable state Enforce rules and carry out collective decisions Public decisions remain promises that officials cannot implement. The rule of law Bind rulers to rules beyond their personal wishes Government can use its power arbitrarily. Accountability Make rulers answer to the people they govern Leaders can ignore public interests without an effective challenge. A state can administer a territory well while giving citizens little control over its decisions. A country can also hold elections while struggling to collect taxes or provide services. Neither achievement guarantees the other.
The rule of law requires more than a written legal code. A ruler who can change or ignore every restriction still stands above the law. Similarly, a ruler’s sincere concern for public welfare differs from institutions that let people enforce accountability. Fukuyama restates these distinctions in “The Patterns of History”.
The Starting Point Is Social Life Fukuyama rejects the picture of early humans as isolated individuals who later chose to form society. Humans inherited social capacities from earlier primates. Family attachments and exchanges of favors helped people cooperate before states existed.
These relationships solve real problems. A kin group can protect its members and organize mutual help. But personal loyalty creates difficulties when public duties extend to strangers. An official may feel obliged to help a relative even when the rules require equal treatment.
Patrimonial government treats political authority as an extension of the ruler’s household. Offices and resources serve family members and personal followers. Impersonal government tries to make appointment and treatment depend on public rules instead.
This transition never becomes permanently secure. Fukuyama’s discussion of military slavery shows how far rulers went to redirect loyalty. Ottoman rulers recruited enslaved outsiders into military and administrative service, separating them from existing kin networks. The method’s coercion is part of its history. It illustrates the problem of building loyalty beyond family, not a model for reform. Stanford’s account of the book’s launch covers these arguments.
China: State Capacity Before Constitutional Restraint Ancient China provides Fukuyama’s central example of early bureaucratic government. Intense military competition pushed rulers to mobilize larger armies. That required taxation, records, supply systems, and officials who could manage them.
Under these pressures, administrative ability became more valuable than aristocratic birth alone. Qin unification in 221 BCE marked an important stage in this process. Fukuyama calls the resulting state modern because of its centralized, relatively impersonal administration. He does not mean that it was democratic or that it possessed every feature of a present-day civil service.
The achievement also created a danger. A capable bureaucracy could carry out destructive orders as well as useful ones. Moral instruction might encourage a good emperor, but it could not reliably stop a bad emperor. State capacity had developed without equally strong, independent checks on the ruler.
The point is analytical: administrative strength and freedom need separate explanations. Fukuyama explains the military mechanism and the danger of unchecked rulers in his Carnegie Council presentation.
Religion Could Place Law Above Rulers Fukuyama gives religion a major role in the origins of legal restraint. Sacred rules could claim authority independent of whoever held political office. Priests and jurists could preserve and interpret those rules across changes of government.
In his account of India, Brahmin religious authority stood apart from the military power of rulers. Social and religious institutions limited how completely a king could reorganize society. This helped restrain political power while also making centralized administration harder to build.
In Muslim societies, religious scholars likewise interpreted a body of law that rulers did not simply invent. In medieval Europe, the Catholic Church’s struggle for independence from secular rulers strengthened a separate legal institution. Canon law and trained legal specialists helped make law more systematic and durable. Fukuyama explains these comparisons in his MISTRA lecture.
Legal restraint in this sense does not establish equal rights. A law can constrain a king while preserving inherited status or exclusion. Readers must distinguish the existence of limits on rulers from the fairness of the rules themselves.
Europe: Accountability Grew Out of Political Conflict Fukuyama’s European comparisons show that limiting a monarch did not automatically produce good government. The identity and organization of the groups imposing limits mattered.
England’s Parliament survived attempts to concentrate royal power. Conflict over taxation and authority eventually produced a constitutional settlement that strengthened parliamentary control. This was an important source of accountable government, although Parliament represented a narrow part of society. Popular democracy required later changes.
Elsewhere, different balances produced different outcomes. Strong monarchies could suppress independent resistance. Powerful nobles could also defend privileges while leaving the state too weak to act effectively. An elite’s freedom from royal interference could coexist with domination of ordinary people.
The comparative lesson is that both power and restraint are necessary. A weak government held captive by privileged groups is no more a complete solution than an unchecked monarch. Martin Hewson’s review in Reviews in History discusses these divergent European paths.
Institutions Can Decay Political development can reverse. Fukuyama describes two recurring dangers. Established rules can become poorly suited to new conditions. Public institutions can also become sources of private advantage.
Old-regime France illustrates the second danger. Selling public offices helped the monarchy obtain revenue. But officeholders gained interests in preserving privileges, including arrangements that let offices pass within families. A solution to an immediate financial problem made later reform harder.
This is repatrimonialization: personal and family interests regain control over institutions meant to serve public purposes. It need not involve the disappearance of government. The offices can survive while their function changes.
Decay also reflects institutional rigidity. Rules acquire moral authority, and beneficiaries organize to defend them. Arrangements that once helped solve a problem may therefore survive after conditions change. Fukuyama develops this warning in the publisher’s opening excerpt.
What the Argument Changes About Reform Fukuyama warns against assuming that elections alone will create effective administration. He also doubts that outsiders can transplant successful institutions without understanding local history. His discussion with development practitioners stresses the difficulty of building courts and changing entrenched incentives.
A practical use of the framework is to diagnose failures more precisely. Consider a hypothetical public clinic. Missing supplies may reflect weak purchasing systems, favoritism toward a contractor, or officials who face no pressure to respond. These failures can occur together, but they require different remedies.
This example is an application of the framework, rather than a case from the book. It shows why changing leaders may leave deeper problems untouched. Reform must connect public authority, enforceable rules, and ways for people to challenge failure.
Strengths and Limits The book’s strength is its separation of institutions that are often treated as one package. Its historical comparisons make it harder to assume that wealth, democracy, and administrative competence always advance together.
Its breadth also requires caution. Calling ancient Chinese administration modern highlights an important similarity across eras, but can hide large differences. Broad regional comparisons can obscure variation within India, China, Europe, and the Muslim world. This is a selective explanation of institutional origins, not a complete global history.
My reading is that the framework works best as a set of questions, not a prediction engine. It directs attention to who exercises power, what limits them, and who can demand a response. Historical origins help explain those relationships. They cannot settle how a present institution performs without further evidence.
Sources Francis Fukuyama: book overview and scope. Macmillan: author credit and authorized opening excerpt. Carnegie Council: Fukuyama’s presentation and questions. MISTRA: Fukuyama’s lecture on institutional origins. Additional supporting material is linked beside the relevant discussion: Fukuyama’s essay, Stanford’s launch report, Carnegie Endowment’s event account, and Hewson’s review.
